Confidence intervals for binomial proportions

Source: R/core-stats-prop.R
hr_prop_ci.Rd

Intervals for x successes out of n trials, vectorised over both.

Usage

hr_prop_ci(
  x,
  n,
  method = c("wilson", "clopper_pearson", "jeffreys"),
  side = c("two", "lower", "upper"),
  conf = 0.95
)

Arguments

x

Number of successes: whole numbers from 0 to n.

n

Number of trials: whole numbers. Recycled against x. A row with n = 0 has NA for the estimate and both bounds.

method

One of "wilson", "clopper_pearson" or "jeffreys".

side

"two" for a two-sided interval, "lower" for a lower bound only, "upper" for an upper bound only.

conf

Confidence level, strictly between 0 and 1.

Value

A data frame with one row per element: x, n, est (x / n), lower, upper, method, side and conf.

Details

Which method to use:

  • Wilson (the default) for descriptive rates: a sensitivity, a share of records kept, an error rate reported alongside an estimate. It is close to nominal coverage on average and does not collapse to a point at 0 or n successes.

  • Clopper-Pearson for any "at least" or "at most" guarantee, such as "recall is at least 0.95" or "the error rate is at most 2%". It never covers less than conf, where Wilson can dip below it when x or n - x is 0 to 3 (Brown, Cai and DasGupta 2001).

  • Jeffreys, the equal-tailed interval of the Beta(x + 1/2, n - x + 1/2) posterior, as a middle ground when a one-number comparison with other Bayesian summaries is wanted.

Wilson here has no continuity correction, so the two-sided interval is the one prop.test(x, n, correct = FALSE) reports, with the lower bound exactly 0 at x = 0 and the upper exactly 1 at x = n. The Clopper-Pearson interval is the one binom.test(x, n) reports. The Jeffreys bounds are qbeta(a, x + 0.5, n - x + 0.5) and qbeta(1 - a, x + 0.5, n - x + 0.5), with the lower bound set to 0 at x = 0 and the upper to 1 at x = n.

A one-sided bound spends the whole of 1 - conf on its side: side = "lower" gives [lower, 1] and side = "upper" gives [0, upper], as binom.test(..., alternative = "greater") and "less" do.

References

Brown, L. D., Cai, T. T. and DasGupta, A. (2001). Interval estimation for a binomial proportion. Statistical Science 16(2), 101-133.

Clopper, C. J. and Pearson, E. S. (1934). The use of confidence or fiducial limits illustrated in the case of the binomial. Biometrika 26(4), 404-413.

Wilson, E. B. (1927). Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference. Journal of the American Statistical Association 22(158), 209-212.

See also

Other statistics: hr_agreement(), hr_alt_test(), hr_ht_estimate(), hr_ppi()

Examples

# A descriptive rate: 46 of 50 eligible records were kept.
hr_prop_ci(46, 50)
#>    x  n  est     lower     upper method side conf
#> 1 46 50 0.92 0.8116175 0.9684505 wilson  two 0.95

# A guarantee: is recall at least 0.90? Read the one-sided exact bound.
hr_prop_ci(46, 50, method = "clopper_pearson", side = "lower")
#>    x  n  est     lower upper          method  side conf
#> 1 46 50 0.92 0.8262088     1 clopper_pearson lower 0.95

# Vectorised: three rates at once.
hr_prop_ci(c(0, 5, 20), c(20, 20, 20), method = "jeffreys")
#>    x  n  est     lower     upper   method side conf
#> 1  0 20 0.00 0.0000000 0.1166390 jeffreys  two 0.95
#> 2  5 20 0.25 0.1023985 0.4641946 jeffreys  two 0.95
#> 3 20 20 1.00 0.8833610 1.0000000 jeffreys  two 0.95
